This poem by the Mu'tazilite poet Safwan al-Ansari is an exceptionally important document for understanding the political activity of the Mu'tazilites. We quote the following lines from it:

His men are in every frontier town beyond the people of China, As far as the distant Sous and beyond the Berbers. Men who preach the cause, whose resolve cannot be broken By the scorn of a tyrant or the schemes of a trickster. When called to travel in winter, they willingly go; In summer, too, they fear no scorching month. They leave their homes behind, giving freely and bearing the cost, Facing great dangers and the hardship of the road. He made their efforts prosper and struck a spark from their flint, And kindled a flame of triumph that overpowered their opponents. They are the anchors of God's earth in every town, Its source of counsel and of wisdom in disputes. In every debate they reach the very heart of the matter, As a butcher's blade finds its mark in the bone. You see them as though birds were resting on their heads, Upon turbans known to the communities around them.

Al-Jahshiyari, History of the Ministers, p. 128. Ibn Qutayba relates that Amr ibn Ubayd, the leader of the Mu'tazilites after Wasil, once spoke to al-Mansur. One of the caliph's companions took offence at what Amr said, and al-Mansur fell silent. Pointing at the man, Amr said to al-Mansur: “This man has kept you company for twenty years and has never seen fit to offer you a word of advice. And beyond your door, nothing is being done in accordance with the Book of God or the example of His Prophet.” Al-Mansur replied, “What am I to do? Here, I have put my signet ring in your hand. Come with your companions and relieve me of the burden.” Amr replied, “Call us to your side by acting justly, and we will gladly help you. A thousand wrongs await redress at your door. Put some of them right, and we will know you are sincere.” See Choice Accounts, vol. 3, p. 237. ↩
